clue.text: One of those children of the brave.

definitions.text: One of those children of the brave.

parts.words: One of those children of the brave.
parts.note: a brave is a Native American warrior, so the clue asks for the word for one of their infants, carried on the back

explanation.surface: A patriotic tribute to the offspring of courageous people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The brave' sounds like courageous people in general; here a brave is a Native American warrior.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names a Native American baby, the child of a warrior or brave.

clue.text: It 'should teach one a lesson.

parts.note: read plainly as a threat of punishment, but meant as a story told for its moral

explanation.surface: Someone vows that a punishment will teach a wrongdoer a lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: A moral story, such as those in the Gospels, exists to teach its hearers something.

clue.text: Mount with a variety of rock shape.

indicators.note: a variety is a different arrangement, so the letters of the following words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A climber's mountain combines several kinds of rock formation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' suggests a peak to go with the rock, but it is a beast to ride; 'a variety of' rearranges ROCK SHAPE.
explanation.definitionFit: A pack animal is something you can ride or load, and a mount is any animal ridden.

clue.text: Famous hunter in an all-star show.

definitions.meaning: the giant huntsman of Greek myth
a constellation is a display made entirely of stars

explanation.surface: A celebrated big-game hunter appears in a celebrity-packed show.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek mythological huntsman was set among the stars as a constellation, literally a show of stars.

clue.text: He had his jest, and they had his (Dryden.)

definitions.text: He had his jest, and they had his (Dryden.)

parts.words: He had his jest, and they had his (Dryden.)
parts.note: a line from Dryden with its final word left out; the solver supplies the missing word

explanation.surface: A quotation from the poet Dryden about a man who joked and lost his property.
explanation.walkthrough: The line from Dryden ends 'and they had his estate'; the clue gives the line with its last word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: In Dryden's line, the jester's land and property were taken from him, which completes the quotation.

clue.text: This way "tea-goes into beards.!'

indicators.note: turning one set of letters into a word shows a rearrangement of the hyphenated pair

explanation.surface: A whimsical notion of spilt tea soaking into men's beards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' rearranges the letters of TEA-GOES; 'This way' only introduces the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Small pointed chin tufts are a style of beard, like the one a billy goat has.

clue.text: Appropriate outcome of one talking as me, terrible too!

definitions.text: Appropriate outcome of one talking as me, terrible too!

indicators.note: the letters come out of the run of words that follows, spanning their joins

explanation.surface: A complaint that a chatterbox's talk yields fitting results, terrible as they are.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'talkinG AS ME TERrible'; the whole clue also defines, since one talking produces 'gas' that such a device would fittingly record.
explanation.definitionFit: A meter records gas, and gas is slang for idle talk, so it is the fitting gauge for a chatterbox.

clue.text: Queer cargo, one would think, in ketch.

definitions.text: Queer cargo, one would think, in ketch.

parts.words: Queer cargo, one would think, in ketch.
parts.note: a vegetable with a heart and a choke seems an odd thing to stow aboard a small two-masted sailing boat

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on the strange goods loaded aboard a small sailing vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The thistle-like vegetable is an unlikely load for a ketch, a small two-masted boat, which is the joke of the clue.

clue.text: Lamb like, but I must cut a sort of dash.

indicators.note: a letter that has to cut into a word is placed inside it

parts.note: elan is dash in the sense of verve and flair

explanation.surface: A remark that a gentle manner must give way to some flair.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb is Charles Lamb, who wrote essays as 'Elia'; 'must cut' puts I inside ELAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Lamb's pen name was Elia, so writing in his manner is described with this adjective.

clue.text: You can see definite splits in, to wit, his manuscript.

parts.note: SC is short for scilicet, Latin for to wit or namely

explanation.surface: Disagreements can plainly be seen in someone's handwritten document.
explanation.walkthrough: SC (scilicet) is a dictionary abbreviation meaning 'namely'.
explanation.definitionFit: Divisions within a church or party are formal breaches, or splits.

clue.text: It's an acknowledgment that you've

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'It's an acknowledgment that you've (7)': it stops mid-sentence, a word or more lost after 'you've', and no scan or search gives the rest.

clue.text: Blindly, stupid:? Just the reverse.

parts.note: swap the order to read stupid with being blind, where blind is slang for very drunk

explanation.surface: Someone corrects a description of foolish behaviour by turning it around.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means foolish through habitual drunkenness, and blind is slang for drunk.

clue.text: Certainly an off-stage position.

parts.note: literally a place out of the audience's sight in a theatre, also meaning out of public view

explanation.surface: A remark about where someone stands in a theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means literally backstage, out of view of the audience, as well as secretly.

clue.text: A weird way for things to go.

definitions.text: A weird way for things to go.

parts.words: A weird way for things to go.
parts.note: an adverb describing events proceeding strangely or uncannily

explanation.surface: Someone comments that events are taking a strange turn.
explanation.definitionFit: An uncanny or spooky manner is a weird way of happening.

clue.text: Simply one's utmost — even the top quality.

parts.note: the best is the highest quality

explanation.surface: Doing your utmost is simply a matter of steady top-quality work.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means the greatest effort a person can make.

clue.text: This is really poisonous.!;

parts.note: the word for spiteful talk applies literally to a snake bite carrying toxin

explanation.surface: A warning that something is genuinely toxic.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes creatures that inject toxin, while figuratively it means spiteful.

clue.text: Properly done!

parts.note: done is slang for cheated or tricked, so properly done means thoroughly beaten by cleverness

explanation.surface: An exclamation of praise for a job well carried out.
explanation.definitionFit: To be done is to be fooled, and being thoroughly fooled by someone cleverer is the sense here.

clue.text: Exemplary, anyhow, this clue.

parts.note: the clue calls itself one example of a clue, a sample case

explanation.surface: The setter praises this clue as a model one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exemplary' seems to mean excellent; here it means serving as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A single example or case of something, as this clue is one case of a clue.

clue.text: Hardly, a.procedure librarian.?.

parts.note: putting books on racks is a librarian's routine, though the word also means postponing indefinitely

explanation.surface: Someone doubts that a task belongs to a librarian's routine.
explanation.definitionFit: Librarians place books on racks, and the same word means setting a plan aside.

clue.text: Not many take: in Vera

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Not many take: in Vera (7)': SE(VERA)L needs a piece round VERA that no surviving words give; the clue looks cut short and no scan or search gives the rest.

clue.text: Ready for the punt — no longer unfit.

definitions.meaning: a punt is a bet, so one ready for it is a person who wagers

explanation.surface: A man fit again and ready to go out on a river boat.
explanation.walkthrough: A punt is a wager as well as a flat-bottomed boat.
explanation.definitionFit: One who wagers is a bettor, and someone recovered from illness is improved in health.

clue.text: The spare man's reticence.

definitions.meaning: a substitute kept back in case a player is needed

explanation.surface: A remark on the quietness of the man left on the bench.
explanation.definitionFit: A substitute player is a spare, and restraint in manner is reticence.

clue.text: In which one's likely to meet a poser.

definitions.text: In which one's likely to meet a poser.

parts.words: In which one's likely to meet a poser.
parts.note: a poser seems a puzzle, but here is a model posing for an artist or photographer

explanation.surface: A place where one encounters a tricky question.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist's or photographer's workroom is where models pose.

clue.text: Figuratively speaking: some think them important.

definitions.text: Figuratively speaking: some think them important.

parts.words: Figuratively speaking: some think them important.
parts.note: figure here means body shape, so these are measurements of bust, waist and hips, also key data

explanation.surface: A comment that some people value metaphors.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means key figures such as births and deaths, and jokingly a woman's body measurements.

clue.text: "Didst thou never see —— kiss a dish of butter?" (K. Henry IV, Pt. I.)

definitions.text: "Didst thou never see —— kiss a dish of butter?" (K. Henry IV, Pt. I.)

parts.words: "Didst thou never see —— kiss a dish of butter?" (K. Henry IV, Pt. I.)
parts.note: Falstaff's line in Shakespeare with one word blanked; the missing word names the sun god of Greek myth

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1 with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Falstaff speaks the line in Henry IV Part 1; the gap is the sun, named after Hyperion, one of the race of giant gods of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare calls the sun by the name of that race of giant gods, picturing it melting butter as it shines.

clue.text: Jam up — take hold!

definitions.meaning: of machinery, to stick fast and stop working

explanation.surface: An urgent instruction to grab something stuck.
explanation.definitionFit: An engine that sticks has jammed, and grabbing something is grasping it.

clue.text: Net rate be applied for this fabric.

indicators.note: letters that are applied differently are put to new use, so the pair of words is rearranged

explanation.surface: A trader quotes a net price for a cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be applied' rearranges NET RATE; RATTEEN is an old coarse woollen cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: An old thick twilled woollen cloth is a kind of fabric.

clue.text: One of those currentfollowers.

parts.note: current followers seem people keeping up with fashion, but the sense is one carried along by water

explanation.surface: Someone who follows whatever is in fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as printed runs 'current followers' together.
explanation.definitionFit: A fishing boat with drift nets, or an aimless person, goes with the current.

clue.text: Arch opening moony too!

definitions.meaning: a half-moon window or opening in a vaulted ceiling

explanation.surface: An archway gives a dreamy view.
explanation.definitionFit: The word, from French for little moon, names a crescent-shaped space or window under an arch.

clue.text: Belated feeling of the neglected bowler?

definitions.meaning: a cricket bowler not given a turn feels an over is owed to him

explanation.surface: A tardy feeling of an ignored bowler.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled by one player.
explanation.definitionFit: Late means behind time, and a neglected bowler feels his set of six balls is owed.
